summary:
Sidney Primas, CTO and founder of LemonSlice, frames the company's mission as breaking the Avatar Turing test: producing video avatars indistinguishable from a human on a video call. The launch example is a Teddy Roosevelt avatar in a replica Oval Office built with Microsoft for Roosevelt's presidential library; a real recorded interaction with President Trump lasted about ten minutes, demonstrating that the full-body avatar can sustain multi-minute dialogue in production. Primas argues that most human-AI interactions will eventually include a visual layer because humans process visual information more naturally than text or voice alone.

LemonSlice differentiates by training world models focused on humans rather than building conventional avatar pipelines. This is harder up front but yields emergent capabilities such as full-body movement, hand actions, object interaction, scene motion, physics (e.g., earrings and water responding naturally), and micro-expressions. The product is positioned as an API layer; customers bring their own LLM and voice, and LemonSlice provides the visual layer. Any single image can drive a photorealistic, Pixar-style, or cartoon avatar, and clothing, scene, and style can change within one inference session.

Technically, LemonSlice trains its own video DiT. Audio is treated as critical: most off-the-shelf audio encoders are trained on monotone audiobooks, so LemonSlice builds custom encoders to produce expressive audio embeddings. To make video interactive, the team replaces the model's usual bidirectional attention with a causal attention mask, enforced at training time, and collapses roughly 30 denoising steps down to a single step. The core remaining challenge is error accumulation: each generated block inherits and compounds the errors of previous blocks, which is severe for continuous sessions of 8–16 hours. Primas says they have a novel, undisclosed solution.

Cost has been reduced to roughly that of serving a voice model. The 'model harness' — orchestration of threads and queues across GPU and CPU so video never stutters under interrupts — is positioned as an underexplored source of long-term value. The next milestone is an emotion engine that, given the avatar's audio and text input, predicts the right emotion, action, and duration; this is targeted for one to two months out. Looking further, Primas bets on a single end-to-end 'EQ model' that ingests user video and audio, maintains an internal emotional state in latent space, and outputs avatar video and audio, with a separate IQ model supplying tool-calling and reasoning. He also announces LemonSlice's own Avatar Turing test, planned to run this year with real people, and notes the team is hiring.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: LemonSlice's goal is to break the Avatar Turing test with photorealistic, real-time, full-body video avatars indistinguishable from a human on a video call.
LemonSlice takes a world-model-pointed-at-humans approach, trading harder training and deployment for emergent full-body movement, object interaction, physics, and micro-expressions.
The product is an API visual layer: customers bring their own LLM and voice, and a single input image can produce photorealistic, Pixar-style, or cartoon avatars with changeable clothes and scenes.
Audio is the underappreciated driver of emotion and facial expression, so LemonSlice builds custom audio encoders because off-the-shelf ones are trained on monotone audiobook data.
Real-time interactivity is achieved by training a causal attention mask so the model can only look at past frames and audio, and by collapsing roughly 30 denoising steps down to a single step.
Error accumulation is the central difficulty for real-time video, and production avatars must run continuously for 8 to 16 hours without reset; LemonSlice has a novel, undisclosed suppression method.

Serving cost for real-time video is about the same as serving a voice model despite far heavier pixel output, and Primas expects further cost reductions from algorithm, hardware, and token-based architecture shifts.
The model harness — orchestration of threads, queues, and CPU/GPU scheduling that prevents stutter from interrupts — is positioned as an overlooked source of long-term value.
The next milestone is an emotion engine that predicts the right emotion, action, and duration from audio and text input, targeted for one to two months out.

LemonSlice bets on a future single end-to-end 'EQ model' that ingests user video/audio, maintains an internal emotional state, and outputs avatar video/audio, paired with a separate IQ model for tool-calling and reasoning.

sections.title: Mission: breaking the Avatar Turing test
sections.summary: Primas introduces himself as CTO/founder of LemonSlice and frames the company's mission as building an avatar indistinguishable from a human on a video call, listing the long-tail problems they care about: emotions, object interactions, micro-expressions, and internal state. He previews the talk's structure: technical bet, what is built today, hard problems solved, and the long-term bet.

sections.title: Microsoft partnership and the Teddy Roosevelt Oval Office
sections.summary: LemonSlice's launch with Microsoft brought Teddy Roosevelt to life in a replica Oval Office inside Roosevelt's presidential library for real-time interaction. Real footage shows President Trump conversing with the avatar for about ten minutes instead of the planned one. Primas uses this to introduce the visual layer bet: humans are biologically wired to understand information best when a visual component is present, so most AI-human interactions will include a visual layer in the long term.

sections.title: Approach: pointing a world model at humans
sections.summary: LemonSlice's technical bet is to take world models and focus them on humans, which is harder to train and deploy but yields emergent properties: full-body movement, hands, actions, object interactions, scene movement, micro-expressions, and emotions. A live product demo shows an avatar waving, swapping between photorealistic, Pixar, and cartoon looks from a single image, and changing clothes and scenes within one inference session, with physics on earrings and water.

sections.title: API-layer positioning and the audio problem
sections.summary: LemonSlice positions itself as the visual API layer: customers bring their own LLM and voice. The technical work begins with training an in-house video DiT, where audio is treated as the critical signal for emotions and facial expressions. Most existing audio encoders are trained on monotone audiobooks, so LemonSlice invests in custom encoders to produce expressive audio embeddings that let the video model be expressive.

sections.title: From video model to real-time interactive
sections.summary: Making the model interactive requires replacing its usual bidirectional attention with a causal attention mask, enforced at training time, so the model can only see past audio and frames and never future inputs that do not yet exist. To make generation real time, LemonSlice collapses roughly 30 denoising steps down to a single step, going from pure noise directly to a clean video.

sections.title: Error accumulation as the central difficulty
sections.summary: Because the model only looks backward, every generated block looks at previously generated blocks that already contain error, then adds more error, so errors compound over time. A demo clip of a Stanford ophthalmology speaker shows visible drift as a bad example. The Teddy Roosevelt avatar runs continuously for 8 hours with no reset, and another deployment is being built for 16 hours, making drift suppression critical. Primas says they have a novel, undisclosed method that yields no noticeable error accumulation over very long videos.

sections.title: Hardware optimization, cost parity, and the model harness
sections.summary: To make minutes and hours of generated video cost-effective, LemonSlice shrinks and optimizes the models so that serving cost is roughly the same as serving a voice model despite far heavier pixel output, enabling consumer use cases. Primas expands on the 'model harness' — the orchestration of separate threads, GPU and CPU work, queues, and interrupt handling — as a huge and often-overlooked source of technical challenge and long-term product value for any real-time application.

sections.title: Emotion engine and the next-generation model
sections.summary: Today avatars still feel awkward because they don't emotionally react or truly listen. The next step is an emotion engine that, given the avatar's audio input and the text it will say, predicts the right emotion, action, and duration at the right time. A soccer-goal reaction clip and a reflective FaceTime-style conversation clip illustrate stronger, more natural emotional expression and environment interaction in the next-generation (not yet real-time) model. Primas says the model can already produce these actions; the work is making them controllable and deterministic for real-time conversation. Target is one to two months out.

sections.title: Long-term bet: a single end-to-end EQ model
sections.summary: Primas bets that within two to three years there will be a single end-to-end 'EQ model' that takes user video and audio directly, internally performs audio understanding, generates what to say, models its own internal emotional state, and outputs avatar video and audio. This EQ model will be high on emotional intelligence but a separate IQ model will drive tool-calling, reasoning, and tool use. Internally, the EQ model will maintain an internal state in latent space that defines emotions and goals and tracks them over time, rather than being human-interpretable.

sections.title: Q&A: Turing test, misuse, and cost trajectory
sections.summary: In Q&A, Primas clarifies that LemonSlice is not building a tool for political deception and will not be the operator of such use cases. They are designing their own Avatar Turing test with real people, plan to run it this year, expect not to pass it yet, and intend to publish it so others can use it. On cost, he reiterates surprise at how inexpensive serving the avatar is — comparable to a voice model — and expects further reductions from algorithm improvements, hardware improvements, and a shift from diffusion toward token-based architectures that would make this style of video generation significantly cheaper. He closes by noting LemonSlice is hiring.

demonstrations: A real recorded interaction between President Trump and the Teddy Roosevelt avatar inside a replica Oval Office at Roosevelt's presidential library, lasting roughly ten minutes.
A live demo of a full-body avatar waving, with hands, clothing changes, scene changes, and physics on earrings and water within a single inference session.
A single input image driving photorealistic, Pixar-style, and cartoon avatars in turn.
A bad-example clip of an avatar of a Stanford ophthalmology speaker used to visually demonstrate compounding error accumulation over a generated video.
A soccer-goal reaction video showing stronger emotional expression and connection in the next-generation (non-real-time) model.
A reflective FaceTime-style conversation clip showing more natural self-interaction and environment interaction in the next-generation model.
limitations: Error accumulation over long generations causes visible drift if not controlled, and solving it is the core difficulty.
Off-the-shelf audio encoders trained on audiobooks are monotone and insufficient for expressive avatars, forcing custom encoder work.
Lipstick rendering in the live demo was noted to be slightly off due to the AV setup, not the model.
The novel solution to error accumulation was withheld and not disclosed.
The Avatar Turing test is explicitly not yet solved; LemonSlice plans to publish their own version this year.
Today's avatars still feel awkward because they don't emotionally react or truly listen; emotions and actions are described in words rather than tracked as a latent internal state.
Costs still need to fall further for consumer use cases and higher resolution, though Primas expects continued algorithmic and hardware improvements.
quantitativeClaims: The Teddy Roosevelt avatar generates continuously frame-by-frame for 8 hours with no reset.
A second deployment is being built to run for 16 hours straight.
Video denoising is reduced from roughly 30 steps to 1 step for real-time generation.
Serving cost for the video avatar is approximately the same as serving a voice model.
The emotion-engine / next-generation model is targeted for launch in one to two months.
Primas expects end-to-end EQ models to appear on the market within two or three years.
LemonSlice plans to run their own Avatar Turing test this year (and expects not to pass it yet).

Describe how an emotion engine can be layered on top of a video model to control timing, duration, and type of emotion and action.

evidence.excerpt: most audio encoders today are trained on basically audiobooks, which is very monotone, very simple, don't have a a lot of emotions.

evidence.excerpt: we basically train a model with an attention mask so that the model can only look into the past. So, when you do inference, it never can see the future

evidence.excerpt: the model hardness. Um I feel like the model hardness is something that is often overlooked

evidence.excerpt: there is never any stutter that happens inside of the video. Um and this is especially hard when you have things like interrupts, you have queues, you're buffering data, you have to clean the queues.
evidence.supports: Concrete model-harness challenges: stutter prevention, interrupt handling, queue management.
